### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.12.2
on linux_arm64
```

### Terraform Configuration Files

```terraform
import{
to = cloudfoundry_service_instance.one-mds
id = "<instance_id>"
}
```


### Expected Behavior

When using the terraform plan --generate-config-out flag to generate HCL configuration for a resource, I expect the output to include attribute values, even for those marked as sensitive. Currently, these sensitive values are set to ```null```, which limits the usefulness of the generated configuration.

### Actual Behavior

We are using the --generate-config-out flag to generate the HCL configuration for a Cloud Foundry resource. However, the generated configuration contains a null value for the parameters attribute, which is defined as a sensitive attribute in the provider schema.

The relevant part of the resource schema is defined as:

```
"parameters": schema.StringAttribute{
    MarkdownDescription: "A JSON object that is passed to the service broker for managed service instance.",
    Optional:            true,
    Sensitive:           true,
    CustomType:          jsontypes.NormalizedType{},
},
```
To import the resource, we used the following block:

```
import {
  to = cloudfoundry_service_instance.one-mds
  id = "<instance-id>"
}
```

where instance-id is the actual ID of the service instance.

Despite the successful import, the sensitive parameters field is set to ```null``` in the generated configuration, resulting in an incomplete representation of the resource state.

### Steps to Reproduce

1) Lets have a resource where one of the attribute is set as sensitive in schema. In our case it is cloud foundry service instance. So we have a cloud Foundry resource with a parameters attribbute marked as Sensitive: true in the provider schema:

```
"parameters": schema.StringAttribute{
    MarkdownDescription: "A JSON object that is passed to the service broker for managed service instance.",
    Optional:            true,
    Sensitive:           true,
    CustomType:          jsontypes.NormalizedType{},
},
```

2) Add an import block to bring the existing resource into the Terraform state:

Example config:

```
import{
to = cloudfoundry_service_instance.one-mds
id = "<instance-id>"
}
```

3) Run the following command to generate the HCL configuration:

```terraform plan --generate-config-out=resource.tf" ```

4) Open the resource.tf file and inspect the value of the parameters field. values for sensitive parameters will be set to null. The following is a snippet of the generated configuration.
```
# __generated__ by Terraform from "1a2b3c4d-1a2b-1234-acef-12345678"
resource "cloudfoundry_service_instance" "one-mds" {
  annotations       = null
  credentials       = null # sensitive
  labels            = null
  name              = "one-mds-test"
  parameters        = null # sensitive
  route_service_url = null
  service_plan      = "123df34-6t6c-4rf4-44fe-a34f4t553f54"
  space             = "145df34-6t6c-4rf4-44fe-a34f4t553f54"
  syslog_drain_url  = null
  tags              = null
  timeouts          = null
  type              = "managed"
}
```

### Additional Context

We observed that when the Sensitive: true flag is removed from the parameters attribute in the provider schema, the --generate-config-out command successfully includes the actual value of the parameters field in the generated configuration.

This suggests that the omission of the value (i.e., setting it to null) is directly related to the Sensitive setting in the schema. While it’s understandable to avoid exposing sensitive values by default, we can include sensitive values when an explicit flag is passed (e.g., --include-sensitive)

### References

Complete code of the resource available [here](https://github.com/cloudfoundry/terraform-provider-cloudfoundry/blob/main/cloudfoundry/provider/resource_service_instance.go)

Terraform Version

 

 Use Cases

Terraform's import blocks are a powerful addition for managing resource imports declaratively. However, they currently lack support for specifying provider configurations—such as region or alias—which significantly limits their usability in multi-region or multi-account setups.

This limitation is especially impactful for providers like AWS, where resources are region-specific. While AWS Provider v6 introduced dynamic region support directly in resource blocks, import blocks still rely on the default provider configuration. As a result, importing resources that exist in a different region than the default provider requires manual CLI-based workarounds, which break the declarative workflow and complicate automation.

A common pattern in Terraform is using for_each or count to manage infrastructure across multiple regions. For example, a resource block might dynamically create resources in different AWS regions based on input variables. However, when importing existing resources into such a block, the import block has no way to specify the region or provider context for each item.

This becomes a major issue when the resource being imported is located in a region different from the default provider. Without the ability to specify the region in the import block, users are forced to fall back to CLI-based imports or restructure their configuration to use aliased providers—both of which reduce clarity, scalability, and automation potential.

Adding support for a region argument (or provider reference) in import blocks would align them with the flexibility already available in resource blocks and modules, and would make multi-region imports fully declarative and automatable.

 Attempted Solutions

Tried using terraform import CLI with -provider flags, but this doesn't integrate well with import blocks and doesn't scale well in automated or multi-region environments.
 

 Proposal

Option 1: Direct Provider Reference in import Block
Allow import blocks to accept a provider argument, similar to resource blocks:
 

Option 2: Region-Based Provider Resolution (AWS Provider v6 Style) --- PREFERRED METHOD
Follow the pattern introduced in AWS Provider v6, where the region can be specified directly in the resource block, and the provider dynamically configures itself accordingly. Extend this behavior to import blocks by allowing a region argument that informs Terraform which region to target during import.

 

 References

None found at this time.

### Attempted Solutions

Tried using terraform import CLI with -provider flags, but this doesn't integrate well with import blocks and doesn't scale well in automated or multi-region environments.
```
provider "aws" {
  alias  = "us_east_1"

}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "us_west_2"
  region = "us-west-2"
}

  provider = aws.us_west_2
  bucket   = "my-west-bucket"
}

  to = aws_s3_bucket.example
  id = "my-west-bucket"
  # No way to specify provider = aws.us_west_2
}
```

### Proposal

**Option 1:** Direct Provider Reference in import Block
Allow import blocks to accept a provider argument, similar to resource blocks:
```
import {
  to       = aws_s3_bucket.example
  id       = "my-west-bucket"
  provider = aws.us_west_2
}
```

Unfortunately parsing the `terraform apply` output isn't an easy thing to do. We have to use regular expression like so:

```
    # Patterns to match Terraform resource operations
    # These patterns match the typical Terraform apply output format
    patterns = {
        'create': r'# (.+?) will be created',
        'modify': r'# (.+?) will be updated in-place',
        'destroy': r'# (.+?) will be destroyed',
        'replace': r'# (.+?) must be replaced'
    }
    
    # Also look for completed operations
    completed_patterns = {
        'create': r'(.+?): Creating\.\.\.',
        'modify': r'(.+?): Modifying\.\.\.',
        'destroy': r'(.+?): Destroying\.\.\.',
        'replace': r'(.+?): Creating\.\.\.'  # Replacement shows as creating
    }
    
    # Parse resource changes from both planned and completed operations
    for action, pattern in {**patterns, **completed_patterns}.items():
        matches = re.findall(pattern, output_content, re.MULTILINE)
        for match in matches:
            resource_full_name = match.strip()
            
            # Extract resource type and name
            # Format is typically: resource_type.resource_name
            if '.' in resource_full_name:
                resource_type, resource_name = resource_full_name.split('.', 1)
                
                # Extract provider (typically the first part before underscore)
                provider = resource_type.split('_')[0] if '_' in resource_type else resource_type
                
                # Try to extract resource ID from output
                resource_id = extract_resource_id(output_content, resource_full_name)
                
                resource_changes.append({
                    'resource_type': resource_type,
                    'provider': provider,
                    'resource_name': resource_name,
                    'resource_id': resource_id,
                    'action': action,
                    'full_name': resource_full_name
                })
```

I propose that `terraform apply` be given an option to output a machine-readable report of all the actions that it has taken. I envisage this being similar in syntax to `terraform plan`'s [-out option](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan#out-filename) which can be converted to JSON (`terraform show -json tfplanfile.out`).

We could then read the file and easily parse out all the actions and store the information in our data store.

```
variable "users" {

}

  for_each = var.users

  name         = "tenants--${each.key}--${each.value.userid}"
```

### Terraform Version

```shell
latest
```

### Use Cases

Currently, Terraform disallows ephemeral values in non-write-only attributes. However, many resources produce a mix of values, some that should not be stored in state (ephemeral, often sensitive), and others that must persist in state to be useful.

Examples:
1. `tls_private_key`
    - Private key PEM → should remain ephemeral (used at apply time only).
    - Public key → often needs to stick around in the state and be passed around to various places.
2. `vault_kv_secret_v2`
    - Secret data payload → should remain ephemeral, never written to state.
    - Metadata (e.g., version) → often useful for triggers or referencing in other resources, but currently cannot persist without persisting the entire secret block.

Without a way to selectively mark attributes as ephemeral vs. persistable, users are forced into unsafe or awkward workarounds.

### Attempted Solutions

- Writing secrets into local files with null_resource and local-exec.
- Re-fetching public/metadata values with external data sources
- Accepting that secrets leak into the state file
- Generating keys by hand/externally

### Proposal

Introduce a mechanism to opt in to persisting only selected values in state while treating others as ephemeral.

Two possible designs:

### Design 1: New function: nonephemeral()
Mark an expression as explicitly allowed to persist in state, while sibling attributes remain ephemeral.

```terraform
ephemeral "tls_private_key" "deploy" {
  algorithm = "ED25519"
}

# Persist public key, do not persist private key
resource "google_compute_instance" "instance" {
  ...
  metadata.ssh-keys= nonephemeral(ephemeral.tls_private_key.deploy.public_key_openssh)
}
```
Vault example:
```terraform
ephemeral "vault_kv_secret_v2" "cfg" {
  mount = "kv"
  name  = "app/config"
}

# Persist only metadata.version
resource "google_compute_instance" "instance" {
  metadata.config_version = nonephemeral(ephemeral.tls_private_key.deploy.public_key_openssh)
}
```

### Design 2: terraform_data opt-in
Make terraform_data to explicitly allow persistence of ephemeral values:

```terraform
ephemeral "tls_private_key" "deploy" {
  algorithm = "ED25519"
}

resource "terraform_data" "ssh_pubkey" {
  input               = {
    pubkey = ephemeral.tls_private_key.deploy.public_key_openssh
  }
}
```
Vault example:
```terraform
ephemeral "vault_kv_secret_v2" "cfg" {
  mount = "kv"
  name  = "app/config"
}
resource "terraform_data" "ssh_pubkey" {
  input               = {
    pubkey = ephemeral.tls_private_key.cfg.version
  }
}
```

### References

_No response_

### Use Cases

In automated deployments, it's common to package and deploy entire directories (e.g. Lambda functions, Helm charts, etc.). A directory hash can act as a checksum to conditionally run a build for a given package.

Additionally, a directory hash could serve as a fingerprint for a directory to ensure no unexpected changes have occurred and the deployed version matches the intended version.

### Attempted Solutions

I was able to solve for this by combining existing functions intended for individual files:

```terraform
output "sha256" {
  description = "sha256 hash of the directory (sha256 of sha256 of each file in the directory recursively)"
  
  value = sha256(join("", [
    for file in fileset(var.directory, "**") :
    filesha256("${var.directory}/${file}")
  ]))
}
```

While the above solution works, it feels messy and isn't friendly from a human-readable perspective. 

### Proposal

The solution could look similar to the existing file hashing functions and would accept an argument for the path as well as an optional list of glob patterns to include/exclude from the calculation e.g. `dirsha256(path, [patterns])`

Example:

```terraform
output "directory_hash" {
  value = dirsha256("lambda/my-function", ["!features/.*", "!tests/.*"])
}
```

### Use Cases

There are some edge cases when I don't want terraform to **ever** destroy a resource. This includes situations  with regulations where I am required to keep certain resources for n time period. 

### Attempted Solutions

While today I can set sentinel policies or `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` these behaviors prevent also permanently block the rest of the resources my users have built.

You may also mention that a `removed {}` could remove the resource from state. While this achieves the behavior I want it does not allow me to enforce the behavior at a module level. 

### Proposal

What I would like is a way to produce a module that creates a resource that can never be destroyed by users.

Example
```hcl
resource "random_string" "random" {
  length           = 16
  special          = true
  override_special = "/@£$"
}

resource "db_encryption_key" "app" {
  name = "app-${random_string.random.id}"
  lifecycle {
    destroy = false
  }
}
```

In this situation terraform can CRU the `db_encryption_key` but never delete it, instead it removes it from state. This behavior already exists (and is the default) for [removed {}](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments#lifecycle)

Terraform Version

 

 Use Cases

In many real-world infrastructure projects, organizations maintain multiple Terraform repositories that rely on the same provider versions—especially when following a modular or microservices-based architecture. For example:

A company with 10+ Terraform repositories, each provisioning different AWS resources using the same version of the AWS provider (e.g., terraform-provider-aws v6.12.0).

Teams working on CI/CD pipelines where provider binaries are downloaded repeatedly across builds, wasting time and bandwidth.

Local development environments where multiple engineers have to re-download the same large provider binaries in each repo.

Currently, each repository independently downloads and stores the provider in its own .terraform directory. This leads to:

Redundant storage usage: e.g., the AWS provider binary (terraform-provider-aws_v6.12.0_x5) is approximately 740MB in size. With 10 repositories using the same version, that amounts to 7.4 GB of duplicated data.

Inefficient use of bandwidth: identical binaries are downloaded multiple times.

Increased setup time: repeated installation of the same provider version across repositories slows down initialization.

 Attempted Solutions

Some approaches we've considered or tried:

Symbolic Links: Attempted symlinking .terraform/providers across repos. However, this is error-prone and breaks Terraform’s internal dependency management, especially when dealing with checksums, dependency lock files (.terraform.lock.hcl), and version constraints.

Shared Terraform Plugin Cache (TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR): Terraform does offer a plugin cache via the TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR environment variable. While this helps reduce re-downloading, it does not prevent providers from being copied into each repo’s .terraform directory, thus failing to eliminate redundancy in disk space usage.

 Proposal

Introduce a centralized Terraform provider repository/cache directory, with shared usage across multiple Terraform projects on the same machine.

Key Features:

Centralized Provider Directory: Allow specifying a global path (e.g., ~/.terraform/providers/) where Terraform can read and reference providers without duplicating them in each .terraform subdirectory.

Hard-link or Reference System: When initializing a project, Terraform should check the central directory and create a hard link or reference rather than copying the binary. This saves disk space while maintaining compatibility.

Checksum and Lockfile Integration: Ensure compatibility with .terraform.lock.hcl and provider checksum validation so that reproducibility and integrity remain intact.

Backwards Compatibility: Projects that don’t opt into this centralised mode should continue functioning normally using the current behaviour.

Configuration Example (Hypothetical):
 .terraformrc or terraform CLI config
 

 References

### Use Cases

From time to time, there are useful warnings which are output in human-readable format and which are properly designed to grab the attention of a human browsing the output of `terraform show [plan-file]`. One such useful output is the warning that the plan includes destruction of an imported resource:
```
  # module.vpc.aws_nat_gateway.this[0] must be replaced
  # (imported from "nat-01123")
  # Warning: this will destroy the imported resource
-/+ resource "aws_nat_gateway" "this" {
      ~ allocation_id                      = "eipalloc-34456" -> (known after apply) # forces replacement
      ~ association_id                     = "eipassoc-45567" -> (known after apply)
        connectivity_type                  = "public"
      ~ id                                 = "nat-01123" -> (known after apply)
      ~ network_interface_id               = "eni-24466" -> (known after apply)
      ~ private_ip                         = "a.b.c.10" -> (known after apply)
      ~ public_ip                          = "x.y.z.12" -> (known after apply)
        region                             = "us-east-1"
      ~ secondary_allocation_ids           = [] -> (known after apply)
      ~ secondary_private_ip_address_count = 0 -> (known after apply)
      ~ secondary_private_ip_addresses     = [] -> (known after apply)
      ~ subnet_id                          = "subnet-35577" -> (known after apply) # forces replacement
    }

```
Depending on the nature of the imported+destroyed resource, this could be quite impactful if the warning is missed or swallowed due to custom `jq` commands parsing `terraform show -json` output and not expecting the possibility of warnings in these spots (since they are unusual).

Ultimately, I would like to browse the output of `terraform show` for a large plan one resource at a time, without having to use Find string functionality of my terminal to scroll through potentially thousands of lines of output. I also want to surface all warnings to the reviewer of the plan file contents.

### Attempted Solutions

```
> terraform show the_plan | grep 'this will destroy the imported resource'
  # Warning: this will destroy the imported resource
  # Warning: this will destroy the imported resource
  # Warning: this will destroy the imported resource
> cat the_plan | grep 'this will destroy the imported resource'  # empty output
> terraform show -json the_plan | grep 'this will destroy the imported resource'  # empty output
> 
```

### Proposal

Add support for the `-target=` param to the `terraform output` command such that it behaves similar to `terraform plan -target=`.

### References

[https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/11684](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/11684#issuecomment-528857171) mentions the presence of an existing issue asking for this feature request, but I was unable to locate it.

### Use Cases

If we have a conflicting lock, terraform shows the following message.

```
Error message: writing "[somewhere].tflock"
failed: googleapi: Error 412: At least one of the pre-conditions you
specified did not hold., conditionNotMet

  ID:        8888888888888888

  Info:      
```

We can check this conflicting lock by contacting with a `Who` of that message.
But if terraform is triggered by CI, we can't contact with `Who`.
Because, user of `Who` is a user name of host computer that runs CI.
https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/a4cc769e5bea770aa5cdb5d726a3fe401f906c71/internal/states/statemgr/locker.go#L161

If we can configure `Who`, we can configure CI to use that variable to indicate the person who is responsible for the state lock.

We can't configure `Who` since it's fixed to os user name.
https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/a4cc769e5bea770aa5cdb5d726a3fe401f906c71/internal/states/statemgr/locker.go#L161

When writing big numbers it is hard to visually see what number it is. For a concrete example, the terraform-aws-provider supports the cloudwatch_metric_alarm resource which has a field called threshold (see 

You can use this resource to create an alert in AWS Cloudwatch if a specific value does not pass the check. In case of storage, the value has to be written in bytes. Representing a GB will make your write a number such as 1000000000 which is really hard to read. You could work around it by doing 1000 1000 1000 instead.

The same is true for numbers that represent seconds in resources. Usually its better to do a calculation to make the user aware of that fact.

 Attempted Solutions

As mentioned above, instead of writing the number, it can be replaced with a calculation that represents the number e.g.
1000000000 -> 1000 1000 1000
86400 -> 60 60 24

Before I propose a solution, please be aware of the following:

Neither go nor JSON natively support a way to "pretty-print" numbers in code. Thus, it would be a custom feature to terraform/HCL to recognize such numbers.

Proposal:
Allow numbers to be written in a way that separates the value of thousand for better readability of the code. Which separator to be used is up to the implementation.

Suggestions are , (C, Python), ' or _.

 Use Cases

I have a use-case where I need to occasionally taint a resource so that it gets recreated. To give a little bit of detail, we create some azure postgres flexible servers with HA enabled and configured terraform as an admin with the azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_active_directory_administrator resource so that terraform can login to the server with the cyrilgdn/postgresql provider using an entra token instead of a password. This works well until the DB server fails over to the standby server. The standby, for whatever reason, doesn't have the administrators defined, so we had to taint the resource in terraform state in order to have the resource created again on the standby.

 Attempted Solutions

I tried to setup something to detect when the zone changes and recreate the ad administrator resources, but it is a bit brittle, and if it's pushed to try to recreate the resources in question when no failover has occurred, then the delete API just hangs indefinitely (seemingly due to ownership of objects, but that is debatable), ultimately resulting in a terraform timeout. So the answer to this that seems most obvious to me to both avoid needing to run imperative commands, and avoid this timeout, is to simply put a boolean flag in the lifecycle block that simply tells terraform to recreate the resource.

Alternatively, I need to write removed {} blocks when a server fails over, then run terraform apply to remove those resources from state, then remove those removed {} blocks and run another terraform apply to recreate those resources.

 Proposal

It would be very useful to us if we have something like a boolean lifecycle.tainted meta argument that we can set to true or false in the code for the resource to let terraform know to mark the resource tainted and recreate it when we need to, without having to use the imperative terraform taint command.

 References

hashicorp/terraform-provider-azurerm24736 details the failure to destroy the azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_active_directory_administrator resources.

 Use Cases

Currently, when Terraform initializes a provider, it spawns the provider plugin as a child process. By default, this child process inherits the entire environment context of the parent terraform CLI process.

This means that if I run terraform apply, every configured provider (AWS, Azure, Kubernetes, etc.) has visibility into every environment variable present in the shell (e.g., GITHUB_TOKEN, AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, ARM_CLIENT_ID), regardless of whether that specific provider needs them.

---

The current behavior violates the principle of Least Privilege and leads to configuration conflicts in complex environments:

1. Security/Leakage: A compromised or malicious provider plugin (or a third-party community provider) theoretically has access to credentials meant for other providers (e.g., a Datadog provider process can read my AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY).
2. Implicit Auth Conflicts: When using multiple aliases for the same provider (e.g., aws.prod and aws.dev), accidentally set shell variables (like AWS_PROFILE) can override explicit HCL configurations if the provider precedence logic favors environment variables.
3. CI/CD Hygiene: In CI pipelines where many secrets are injected as env vars, it is difficult to isolate which secrets are visible to which step without complex shell wrappers.

 Attempted Solutions

For now the only way to do it is by using remote vault ephemeral data

 Proposal

I propose adding a meta-argument to the provider block (or a global setting) that allows users to explicitly whitelist which environment variables are passed to the plugin process.

If this list is present, the Terraform Core should filter the environment passed to the go-plugin client, sending only the matching keys.

----
 Proposed Syntax
Option 1 (preferred): Allow-list per provider This would be non-breaking. If omitted, behavior defaults to "inherit all."

 

Option 2: Strict Isolation (Boolean) A flag to strictly disable all env var inheritance, forcing the user to rely solely on input variables defined in the HCL.

 

 References

_No response_

### Terraform Version

```shell
1.x
```

### Use Cases

Currently, when Terraform initializes a provider, it spawns the provider plugin as a child process. By default, this child process inherits the entire environment context of the parent terraform CLI process.

This means that if I run terraform apply, every configured provider (AWS, Azure, Kubernetes, etc.) has visibility into every environment variable present in the shell (e.g., `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `ARM_CLIENT_ID`), regardless of whether that specific provider needs them.

---

The current behavior violates the principle of **Least Privilege** and leads to configuration conflicts in complex environments:

1. **Security/Leakage**: A compromised or malicious provider plugin (or a third-party community provider) theoretically has access to credentials meant for other providers (e.g., a Datadog provider process can read my AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY).
2. **Implicit Auth Conflicts**: When using multiple aliases for the same provider (e.g., aws.prod and aws.dev), accidentally set shell variables (like AWS_PROFILE) can override explicit HCL configurations if the provider precedence logic favors environment variables.
3. **CI/CD Hygiene**: In CI pipelines where many secrets are injected as env vars, it is difficult to isolate which secrets are visible to which step without complex shell wrappers.

### Attempted Solutions

For now the only way to do it is by using remote vault ephemeral data

### Proposal

I propose adding a meta-argument to the provider block (or a global setting) that allows users to explicitly whitelist which environment variables are passed to the plugin process.

If this list is present, the Terraform Core should filter the environment passed to the go-plugin client, sending only the matching keys.

----
### Proposed Syntax
**Option 1 (preferred): Allow-list per provider This would be non-breaking. If omitted, behavior defaults to "inherit all."**

```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
  
  # New Feature: Only pass these specific env vars to the plugin process
  # The plugin will not see GITHUB_TOKEN or other unrelated vars.
  allowed_environment_variables = ["AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY", "AWS_SESSION_TOKEN"]
}
```

**Option 2: Strict Isolation (Boolean) A flag to strictly disable all env var inheritance, forcing the user to rely solely on input variables defined in the HCL.**

```hcl
provider "google" {
  project = "my-project"
  
  # New Feature: The plugin process starts with an empty environment
  isolate_environment = true 
}
```



### References

A common example is when variables are used as configuration inputs for actions, data sources, or downstream modules, and the source of the value may vary across environments or implementations.

### Use Cases

In some workflows, it is desirable for a variable value to reference a resource or module output indirectly, without hard-coding that reference at the call site.

A common example is when variables are used as configuration inputs for actions, data sources, or downstream modules, and the source of the value may vary across environments or implementations.

Example use case:

- A reusable module or action expects a variable representing a resource-derived value (e.g., a Lambda function name).
- The calling configuration wants to supply that value by reference, not as a literal string.
- Today, variables only support literal defaults or expressions resolvable at variable definition time, not references to resources or modules defined elsewhere in the configuration.

This forces one of the following patterns:

- Threading resource outputs explicitly through every call site
- Duplicating references at usage points
- Avoiding variables altogether and coupling consumers directly to resource names

### Attempted Solutions

I attempted to express a resource output reference as a variable default, for example:

```

variable "aws_lambda_function_name_output_path" {
  description = "Path to the lambda function name output"
  type        = string
  default     = "${aws_lambda_function.example.function_name}"
}
```


However, Terraform treats this as invalid because variables cannot reference resources or module outputs.

I also experimented with escaping the expression so it could be interpreted later, for example:

`default = "$${aws_lambda_function.example.function_name}"`


But this is currently treated as a literal string, with no mechanism for deferred interpolation.

### Proposal

Introduce a supported mechanism for deferred or expression-based variable evaluation, allowing variables to reference resource or module outputs after graph construction, without violating Terraform’s dependency model.

One possible design (illustrative, not prescriptive):

```
variable "aws_lambda_function_name_output_path" {
  type    = string
  default = expr(aws_lambda_function.example.function_name)
}

```

or an explicit opt-in syntax for deferred interpolation:

`default = "$${aws_lambda_function.example.function_name}"`


Under this model:

- The variable value is not resolved during variable loading.
- The value is evaluated during graph execution, similar to how resource arguments are resolved.
- Terraform can still infer dependencies based on the referenced resource or module.

This would allow configurations such as:

```
resource "aws_lambda_function" "example" {
  # ...
}

action "aws_lambda_invoke" "example" {
  config {
    function_name = var.aws_lambda_function_name_output_path
    payload = jsonencode({
      key1 = "value1"
      key2 = "value2"
    })
  }
}
```

without forcing consumers to inline the resource reference directly.

**Why This Is Useful**

- Enables more reusable and decoupled modules
- Reduces repetitive wiring of outputs through multiple layers
- Allows configuration-driven indirection without resorting to locals or hard-coded references
- Preserves Terraform’s dependency graph while improving expressiveness

This feature would be especially useful for:

- Actions and providers that accept resource-derived identifiers
- Meta-modules that orchestrate resources without tightly coupling to them
- Advanced automation workflows where values are selected by configuration rather than structure

### Use Cases

I'm using Terraform to stage VM templates (disk images and configuration) for later replication to multiple VM hosts, for the disk images, I'm creating symlinks and using `rsync -L` to avoid unnecessary copies.

I'm currently creating the symlinks with resources like the following:

```
resource "terraform_data" "disk_symlink" {
  triggers_replace = [
    abspath(local.image_path),
    "${ var.template_dir }/${ local.output_image_name }",
  ]

  input = [
    abspath(local.image_path),
    "${ var.template_dir }/${ local.output_image_name }",
  ]

  provisioner "local-exec" {
    environment = {
      SOURCE = self.output[0]
      DEST = self.output[1]
    }

    command = "mkdir -p \"$(dirname \"$DEST\")\" && ln -s \"$SOURCE\" \"$DEST\""
  }

  provisioner "local-exec" {
    when       = destroy
    on_failure = continue

    environment = {
      DEST = self.output[1]
    }

    command = "rm -f \"$DEST\""
  }
}
```

This works and updates the symlink when either the source or destination is changed, but it doesn't gracefully handle either the link pre-existing, or being deleted by something outside of Terraform.

### Attempted Solutions

See above.

### Proposal

It would be nice if there was a `local_symlink` resource which integrated what the above example does and also correctly fixes the state when something else creates/deletes/changes the link.

```
resource "local_symlink" "foo" {
  target = "foo"
  filename = "${path.module}/foo.bar"
}
```

 Use Cases

Organizations that already run Elasticsearch as core infrastructure need a way to store Terraform remote state without introducing additional services. Currently, teams in this situation are forced to stand up a separate storage system (e.g. S3, Consul, Postgres) solely for Terraform state, adding operational overhead, additional credentials to manage, and another point of failure.

 Attempted Solutions

The closest existing option is the http backend, which could theoretically work by placing an HTTP proxy in front of Elasticsearch. However, this approach requires:
1. Writing and maintaining a separate intermediary service that translates between the HTTP backend protocol and Elasticsearch's API
2. Deploying and operating that service as additional infrastructure
3. Implementing state locking manually in the proxy layer, since the HTTP backend's locking support is limited

This defeats the purpose of using existing infrastructure -- it just trades one dependency (a state backend) for another (a custom proxy).

Example of what this workaround looks like:

 

The consul and pg backends serve as precedent for supporting infrastructure that teams already operate. Elasticsearch falls into the same category.

 Proposal

A native elasticsearch backend that stores state as documents in an Elasticsearch index. Configuration would look like:

 

Key design points of the implementation:
- Authentication: Supports username/password, API key, and bearer token (mutually exclusive, validated at configure time)
- TLS: Supports custom CA certificates, client certificates for mutual TLS, and skip-verification -- all via file paths or inline PEM, plus environment variable overrides
- Locking: Uses Elasticsearch's op_type=create for atomic lock acquisition -- no external lock service needed
- Workspaces: Each workspace gets its own state and lock document within the same index, identified by state-{workspace} and lock-{workspace} document IDs
- Index management: The backend auto-creates the index with appropriate mappings on first use
- Environment variables: All configuration fields can be set via ELASTICSEARCH_ environment variables
 
I have a working implementation with full test coverage and am willing to maintain this backend long-term. I'd like to add myself to CODEOWNERS for this backend.

The CONTRIBUTING.md notes that the team is not currently merging new state storage backends. I'm opening this issue to discuss whether an exception is possible given the willingness to maintain it long-term.

Existing community-maintained backends (pg, cos) serve as precedent for third-party-maintained backends in the repository.

- Index management: The backend auto-creates the index with appropriate mappings on first use

### Terraform Version

```shell
1.14.6
```

### Use Cases

Terraform currently requires `count` or `for_each` to conditionally create resources or modules. Both approaches introduce indexing into the resource address (e.g., resource.name[0]), even when managing a single optional instance.

This behavior complicates configuration design, increases cognitive load, and makes refactoring more error-prone.

This request proposes introducing a native mechanism (e.g., enabled meta-argument) to conditionally create resources without changing their state address.

### Attempted Solutions

Today, conditional resource creation is typically implemented as:
```
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
  count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0
}
```

This results in:

`aws_s3_bucket.example[0]`

instead of:

`aws_s3_bucket.example`

### Key limitations:

1. **State address instability**
   - Introducing conditional logic requires changing resource addresses
   - Leads to state migrations or resource recreation risks

2. **Cascading complexity**
   - All dependent resources must reference indexed instances:
     ```hcl
     aws_s3_bucket.example[0].id
     ```
   - Requires conditional guards across the codebase

3. **Refactoring overhead**
   - Converting an existing resource into a conditional one forces address changes
   - Requires `terraform state mv` or manual intervention

4. **Mental overhead**
   - Engineers must always reason about indices, even for single-instance resources



### Proposal

Introduce a meta-argument (name TBD), for example:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
  enabled = var.enabled
}
```

or:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
  condition = var.enabled
}
```

### Expected behavior:

- `enabled = true` → resource is created as:
  ```
  aws_s3_bucket.example
  ```
- `enabled = false` → resource is not created
- No index (`[0]`) is introduced
- Resource address remains stable across lifecycle changes

---

## Design Considerations

### 1. State model

- Resource address should remain constant
- When disabled, resource is absent from state
- Re-enabling recreates the resource at the same address

---

### 2. Dependency handling

Terraform could:

- treat disabled resources as non-existent nodes in the graph
- surface clear errors if referenced while disabled

---

### 3. Backward compatibility

- No breaking changes required
- `count` / `for_each` remain fully supported
- New meta-argument is additive

---

### 4. Module support

The same mechanism should apply to modules:

```hcl
module "example" {
  source  = "./module"
  enabled = var.enabled
}
```

---

## Alternatives Considered

### `count`

- Introduces indexing
- Breaks address stability
- Adds complexity for single-instance use cases

### `for_each`

- Better semantics for collections
- Still introduces keyed addressing
- Overkill for simple boolean conditions

---

## Benefits

- Stable resource addressing
- Simplified configuration
- Easier refactoring of existing infrastructure
- Reduced cognitive overhead
- Cleaner module interfaces
- Improved readability and maintainability

---

## Additional Context

This limitation becomes more apparent in:

- large modular infrastructures
- long-lived Terraform states
- environments with frequent feature toggling
- identity and access management scenarios

This would match the emerging consensus in the industry that upgrading to very recent releases poses an increasing risk of supply-chain attacks. Having a cooldown / minimum age period would give the community time to detect such attacks. Terraform is a tempting target since it is typically run with high-privilege credentials.

 Attempted Solutions

n/a

 Proposal

Add an option (via the usual CLI / config file / environmental variables) to set a minimum age to consider when evaluating module versions (e.g. “Do not install anything released in the last 7 days”). When running terraform init --upgrade the solver can ignore versions which were published after the cutoff date.

To allow high-priority updates or safe sources, it would be useful to implement an exclude mechanism either by disabling this feature for a single provider or module such as a trusted internal publisher or to define the logic such that it only applies when attempting to upgrade the pinned versions but never prevents a newer version when explicitly pinned in the provider / module version (e.g. version = "1.2.3" does not have the check applied but version = "~> 1.2" would treat yesterday's 1.2.3 as if it was never published and use last week's 1.2.2).

### Terraform Version

```shell
v1.15.0
```

### Use Cases

Allow `terraform validate` command to succeed without required validation of backend like s3 in AWS.
Especially useful in CI/CD where the backend is often supplied in the pipeline, rather than hardcoded in .tf files.

Currently we keep backend block empty:

```tf
  backend "s3" {
    # We build it inside CI/CD
  }
```

And in CICD run:

```yaml
          terraform init \
            -backend-config="region=${{ inputs.aws_default_region }}" \
            -backend-config="bucket=${BUCKET_NAME}" \
            -backend-config="key=${KEY_NAME}" \
            -backend-config="use_lockfile=true" \
            -backend-config="encrypt=true"

          terraform validate
```

Which currently fails in `v.1.15.0` with:
```
The argument "bucket" is required, but no definition was found.
The argument "key" is required, but no definition was found.
```

### Attempted Solutions

I tried:

1) ❌ 
```bash
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
```

2) ❌ 
```bash
tfdata="$(mktemp -d)"
TF_DATA_DIR="$tfdata" terraform init -backend=false
TF_DATA_DIR="$tfdata" terraform validate
```

3) ✅ 

```tf
  backend "s3" {
    # We build it inside CI/CD
    bucket = "something"
    key    = "something"
    region = "something"
  }
}
```

```bash
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
```

This succeeded but requires me to touch all our microservice repositories to change empty backend to fake backend.
Highly boring task.

### Proposal

Allow a flag for `terraform validate` command like:

```bash
terraform validate -no-backend
```

To skip this particular validation as it is supplied in GitHub Actions or other CI/CD tool.

Terraform Version

 

 Use Cases

The canonical pattern for managing write-only secret values in Terraform — straight from the docs on ephemeral values — combines:

 

This shape gives the user three desirable properties at once: the random value never enters state, the secret is encrypted with a caller-supplied KMS key, and rotation is handled by bumping a _wo_version integer. Wrapping it into a small helper module so multiple consumer modules can reuse it is the obvious next step.

Once that helper exists, consumers want to test that they wire it correctly. The most common security-relevant invariant is "the helper is invoked with the right kms_key_id" — easy to assert structurally if the test framework can plan / apply the consumer under mock_provider. Today it cannot. The first parse of the helper trips the diagnostic below, regardless of which assertion the test was going to make. Every downstream module that depends on the helper is uniformly untestable.

The pattern isn't niche: any module that surfaces a random-generated secret value (RDS master password, OAuth client credentials, OIDC cookie key, …) follows the same shape; the testing gap blocks all of them.

 Attempted Solutions

We tried, in order:

1. Module-local tests for the helper itself — command = apply with mock_provider. The error fires at module-load time, before any run block executes:
 
2. Plan-only tests — command = plan. Same diagnostic; the rejection isn't apply-specific.
3. override_module on the helper from the consumer module's tests:
 
 The module is still loaded for type-checking before the override applies, so the ephemeral block is still parsed and the diagnostic still fires. The override has no effect on the rejection.
4. Variable-level validation tests — validation {} blocks inside variable "X" are testable via expect_failures at command = plan because the variable is evaluated before the resource graph is walked. We use this for "is kms_key_id non-null" type invariants. But it cannot cover invariants that live on resource attributes (the actual kms_key_id value flowing into aws_secretsmanager_secret, downstream wiring of secret_arn into IAM grants, etc.) — those require an actual plan, which is what's blocked.
5. Falling back to make env. .check against the real AWS provider on a host with credentials. Works, but moves the assertion from CI-friendly terraform test into an SSO-driven manual workflow, with the security-relevant invariants only checked by humans at PR-review time.

None of these close the gap for consuming modules that need to assert on resource-level attributes inside an ephemeral-using helper.

 Proposal

Extend mock_provider so ephemeral resource types follow the same model as managed resources:

- mock_resource blocks accept defaults for ephemeral types, returning the configured values from OpenEphemeralResource and the appropriate empty / no-op responses from RenewEphemeralResource and CloseEphemeralResource. Example:
 
- override_resource blocks accept ephemeral resource addresses, overriding the mock defaults for a specific instance, same syntax as managed resources today.
- ValidateEphemeralResourceConfig returns no diagnostics under the mock provider, leaving validation to the consumer's own logic.

Concretely, in internal/providers/mock.go, the four ephemeral protocol methods today return the same hard-coded diagnostic; three carry a FIXME: Design some means to mock an ephemeral resource type. comment (introduced 2024-09-13 in 3b77e57ce4854820411134caf44361d48e75ce83). Replacing those stubs with the same Mock / Resources / Overrides plumbing the managed-resource methods already use would close the gap symmetrically.

We do not have a preference between "default to a generated mock value of the correct type" vs. "require the user to set mock_resource defaults explicitly". The first is more ergonomic; the second is more predictable. Either is dramatically better than the current state, where no path through the test framework reaches the consuming module's resources.

 References

- internal/providers/mock.go — FIXME: Design some means to mock an ephemeral resource type. introduced in commit (2024-09-13). This is the closest thing to a tracking artefact for the work; a GitHub-issue search for "mock_provider ephemeral" / "No ephemeral resource types in mock providers" returns no issue or PR as of the date this request is filed.
- — protocol-symbol rename adding Resource suffix (OpenEphemeral → OpenEphemeralResource, etc.); cleans the API surface around which a mock implementation would be written, but doesn't itself touch the mock stubs.
- — adds ValidateEphemeralResourceConfig to the interface, completing the protocol surface for both the real and mock implementations.
- Related but distinct: (open) — root-module terraform validate rejects ephemeral outputs. Different code path, but trips users in similar testing workflows and is worth tracking alongside.
- Unrelated to mocking but found during search, for completeness: hashicorp/terraform35912 (panic on apply, fixed), 36518 (dynamic write-only + nested ephemeral, fixed), 37270 (depends_on on ephemeral resources).

This request was drafted with the help of Claude (Anthropic) in a Claude Code session; the reproducer, code references, and search-for-prior-art steps were verified manually against the linked commits and source.

### Use Cases

The canonical pattern for managing write-only secret values in Terraform — straight from the docs on ephemeral values — combines:

```hcl
ephemeral "random_password" "this" {
  length = 32
}

resource "aws_secretsmanager_secret" "this" {
  name       = var.name
  kms_key_id = var.kms_key_id
}

resource "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "this" {
  secret_id        = aws_secretsmanager_secret.this.id
  secret_string_wo = ephemeral.random_password.this.result
}
```

This shape gives the user three desirable properties at once: the random value never enters state, the secret is encrypted with a caller-supplied KMS key, and rotation is handled by bumping a `*_wo_version` integer. Wrapping it into a small helper module so multiple consumer modules can reuse it is the obvious next step.

Once that helper exists, consumers want to test that they wire it correctly. The most common security-relevant invariant is "the helper is invoked with the right `kms_key_id`" — easy to assert structurally if the test framework can plan / apply the consumer under `mock_provider`. Today it cannot. The first parse of the helper trips the diagnostic below, regardless of which assertion the test was going to make. Every downstream module that depends on the helper is uniformly untestable.

The pattern isn't niche: any module that surfaces a random-generated secret value (RDS master password, OAuth client credentials, OIDC cookie key, …) follows the same shape; the testing gap blocks all of them.

### Attempted Solutions

We tried, in order:

1. **Module-local tests** for the helper itself — `command = apply` with `mock_provider`. The error fires at module-load time, before any `run` block executes:
   ```
   Error: No ephemeral resource types in mock providers
     with ephemeral.random_password.this,
   The provider mocking mechanism does not yet support ephemeral resource
   types.
   ```
2. **Plan-only tests** — `command = plan`. Same diagnostic; the rejection isn't apply-specific.
3. **`override_module`** on the helper from the consumer module's tests:
   ```hcl
   override_module {
     target = module.helper
     outputs = { secret_arn = "arn:aws:secretsmanager:..." }
   }
   ```
   The module is still loaded for type-checking before the override applies, so the ephemeral block is still parsed and the diagnostic still fires. The override has no effect on the rejection.
4. **Variable-level validation tests** — `validation {}` blocks inside `variable "X"` are testable via `expect_failures` at `command = plan` because the variable is evaluated before the resource graph is walked. We use this for "is `kms_key_id` non-null" type invariants. But it cannot cover invariants that live on resource attributes (the actual `kms_key_id` value flowing into `aws_secretsmanager_secret`, downstream wiring of `secret_arn` into IAM grants, etc.) — those require an actual plan, which is what's blocked.
5. **Falling back to `make env.<env>.check`** against the real AWS provider on a host with credentials. Works, but moves the assertion from CI-friendly `terraform test` into an SSO-driven manual workflow, with the security-relevant invariants only checked by humans at PR-review time.

None of these close the gap for consuming modules that need to assert on resource-level attributes inside an ephemeral-using helper.

### Proposal

Extend `mock_provider` so ephemeral resource types follow the same model as managed resources:

- `mock_resource` blocks accept defaults for ephemeral types, returning the configured values from `OpenEphemeralResource` and the appropriate empty / no-op responses from `RenewEphemeralResource` and `CloseEphemeralResource`. Example:
  ```hcl
  mock_provider "random" {
    mock_resource "random_password" {
      defaults = {
        result = "mock-password-value"
      }
    }
  }
  ```
- `override_resource` blocks accept ephemeral resource addresses, overriding the mock defaults for a specific instance, same syntax as managed resources today.
- `ValidateEphemeralResourceConfig` returns no diagnostics under the mock provider, leaving validation to the consumer's own logic.

Concretely, in `internal/providers/mock.go`, the four ephemeral protocol methods today return the same hard-coded diagnostic; three carry a `FIXME: Design some means to mock an ephemeral resource type.` comment (introduced 2024-09-13 in `3b77e57ce4854820411134caf44361d48e75ce83`). Replacing those stubs with the same `Mock` / `Resources` / `Overrides` plumbing the managed-resource methods already use would close the gap symmetrically.

We do not have a preference between "default to a generated mock value of the correct type" vs. "require the user to set `mock_resource` defaults explicitly". The first is more ergonomic; the second is more predictable. Either is dramatically better than the current state, where no path through the test framework reaches the consuming module's resources.

### References

- `internal/providers/mock.go` — `FIXME: Design some means to mock an ephemeral resource type.` introduced in commit https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/commit/3b77e57ce4854820411134caf44361d48e75ce83 (2024-09-13). This is the closest thing to a tracking artefact for the work; a GitHub-issue search for "mock_provider ephemeral" / "No ephemeral resource types in mock providers" returns no issue or PR as of the date this request is filed.
- https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/commit/9c3dc8f73a21dcac28d754d9e556e4bbc5a1b60a — protocol-symbol rename adding `Resource` suffix (`OpenEphemeral` → `OpenEphemeralResource`, etc.); cleans the API surface around which a mock implementation would be written, but doesn't itself touch the mock stubs.
- https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/commit/c70a885afbd3827b72f26892b9fe6f156e3b9eb7 — adds `ValidateEphemeralResourceConfig` to the interface, completing the protocol surface for both the real and mock implementations.
- Related but distinct: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/38309 (open) — root-module `terraform validate` rejects ephemeral outputs. Different code path, but trips users in similar testing workflows and is worth tracking alongside.
- Unrelated to mocking but found during search, for completeness: hashicorp/terraform#35912 (panic on apply, fixed), #36518 (dynamic write-only + nested ephemeral, fixed), #37270 (`depends_on` on ephemeral resources).

This request was drafted with the help of Claude (Anthropic) in a Claude Code session; the reproducer, code references, and search-for-prior-art steps were verified manually against the linked commits and source.

Terraform Version

 

 Use Cases

Tooling that generates or validates Terraform configuration programmatically - code generators, language servers, linters, module scaffolding tools - discovers what a provider supports by reading terraform providers schema -json. That's how these tools learn about resources, data sources, ephemeral resources, functions, and the provider's own configuration schema today.

The AWS provider recently added support for terraform { provider_meta "aws" { user_agent = [...] } } (hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws45464), letting modules tag their own attribution string onto the AWS provider's User-Agent header — used for example by terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-rds (terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-rds615) to replace a static resource tag with proper request-level attribution.

Tooling that wants to generate a typed, validated provider_meta block for a given provider (the same way it already generates typed bindings for that provider's resources, data sources, and functions) has no schema to generate against — provider_meta is invisible to terraform providers schema -json, even for providers that implement it. This makes provider_meta the one schema-driven Terraform capability that can't be discovered the same way everything else can.

 Attempted Solutions

Ran terraform providers schema -json against the AWS provider (6.53.0, which implements provider_meta "aws" { user_agent = [...] }) and inspected the full output:
- The per-provider schema object exposes exactly these top-level keys: provider, resource_schemas, data_source_schemas, ephemeral_resource_schemas, functions, list_resource_schemas, action_schemas, resource_identity_schemas. No provider_meta key is present.
- Searched the entire captured JSON file (~19 MB) for the literal string provider_meta. It appears exactly once, and only inside the human-readable description text of the functions.user_agent entry ("...for use with the user_agent argument in the provider or provider_meta block") - not as a structured schema entry.
- Cross-checked this against the documented output fields on the terraform providers schema CLI reference page, which lists provider, resource_schemas, data_source_schemas, ephemeral_resource_schemas, and functions - provider_meta isn't documented as an output field either.
- Confirmed the plugin protocol itself already carries this data: docs/plugin-protocol/tfplugin6.proto's GetProviderSchema.Response defines Schema provider_meta = 5;, a sibling field to Schema provider = 1;. So the provider genuinely returns a real schema for its provider_meta block over gRPC (that's how terraform init/validate type-check the user_agent argument's shape at parse time) — the JSON serialization in terraform providers schema -json just doesn't surface that field.

Without this, tools are left to either hardcode per-provider assumptions about provider_meta block contents, or fall back to an untyped escape hatch - unlike every other schema-driven capability the JSON output already supports.

 Proposal

Add a provider_meta key to the per-provider object in terraform providers schema -json output, as a sibling to the existing provider key, sourced directly from the GetProviderSchema.Response.provider_meta field the plugin protocol already returns. Suggested shape - the same block/attributes schema representation already used for provider:

 

When a provider defines no provider_meta schema, this key would presumably be omitted for that provider, consistent with how other optional schema sections already behave.

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.15.8
on windows_amd64
+ provider registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws v6.56.0
```

### Use Cases

When developing modules, it is often convenient to output one or more complete resources as output fields, instead of individual fields. This helps the module remain useful without needing consistent updates when fields are added or removed from individual resources.

For example, if I have a module that creates an S3 bucket and configures replication on it, it may contain:

`bucket.tf`
```
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
  bucket = "my-tf-test-bucket"

  tags = {
    Name        = "My bucket"
    Environment = "Dev"
  }
}

output "bucket" {
  value = aws_s3_bucket.example
}
```

This allows the user of the module to then access whatever fields on the bucket they like (e.g. `bucket_regional_domain_name`), and new fields added in new provider versions will be available without needing to modify the module.

A recent change (I'm not sure when exactly this changed, but it's an issue as of Terraform v1.15.8) has caused this to log deprecation warnings for every deprecated field on the resource in the `output`. In the example above, it will cause a deprecation warning like this:

```
Warning: Deprecated value used
│ 
│   on bucket.tf line 11, in output "bucket":
│   11:   value       = aws_s3_bucket.example
│ 
│   The deprecation originates from aws_s3_bucket.example.website_domain
│ 
│ website_domainis deprecated. [more deprecation instructions here]
│ 
│ (and 13 more similar warnings elsewhere)
```

### Attempted Solutions

My module now filters out all deprecated fields like so:

```
output "bucket" {
  description = "The `aws_s3_bucket` resource that was created."
  value = {
    for k, v in aws_s3_bucket.example :
    k => v
    if !contains(
      [
        "acceleration_status",
        "acl",
        "grant",
        "cors_rule",
        "lifecycle_rule",
        "logging",
        "object_lock_configuration",
        "policy",
        "replication_configuration",
        "request_payer",
        "server_side_encryption_configuration",
        "versioning",
        "website",
        "website_domain",
        "website_endpoint",
    ], k)
  }
}
```

But this is obviously not sustainable as it requires a new release of the module for every deprecation change.

### Proposal

Ignore deprecation warnings for `output` values. Or, if that's too broad, ignore deprecation warnings when an entire resource is being referenced and not an individual attribute.

Terraform Version

 

 Use Cases

I run Terraform drift checks on a schedule and in CI, across a lot of workspaces. I want them to fire only when something has actually changed outside of Terraform, and to never be able to change anything themselves.

Detection isn't the missing piece, though it's fiddly. terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode already returns exit 2 only when there's drift (an unapplied config change doesn't trigger it), and -json emits resource_drift, but you have to know that exact flag combination and parse the JSON to see what actually changed. Two bigger things are the problem.

First, I can't tell a check to ignore drift I already know about, just for that run. There's always some noise, like a tag a scanner rewrites every hour or an attribute the provider keeps normalizing. My only knob today is ignore_changes, and it's the wrong tool for an alarm (more on that below). So I either get paged for noise or mute the whole resource and miss real drift on it.

Second, the check isn't guaranteed read-only. I'm running plan, which takes -out and is one step from something appliable. I'd be a lot more comfortable scheduling that across dozens of workspaces, or handing it to compliance, if it simply couldn't change anything.

 Attempted Solutions

For finding drift the refresh-only route is fine.

 

It's the suppression part that breaks down. Take that scanner rewriting tags["LastScanned"] every hour, so every run lights up on it. Right now I have two options.

- Put ignore_changes = [tags["LastScanned"]] in the config. That quiets the alarm, but now apply won't reconcile that tag either, it needs a review, and it's global, not scoped to this one check.
- Filter the -json in jq and work out the exit code myself. That's a fragile script I have to babysit per resource type.

Neither lets me ignore that one tag for this check while still failing on any other drift.

I also looked at terraform refresh, but it does the opposite of what I need here. It writes the drifted values into state, which erases the very drift I'm trying to detect.

 Proposal

I'd propose a terraform drift command. What makes it more than a wrapper around plan -refresh-only is a -ignore flag that hides expected drift from the report, and only the report.

terraform drift -ignore=aws_s3_bucket.demo drops a whole resource; -ignore='aws_instance.web:tags["LastScanned"]' drops one attribute. The address is just the normal resource instance address you already use in plan output and -target (count/for_each and modules work, managed resources only), and the attribute part is the same syntax as ignore_changes. It only affects what's printed, never state, never infra, never what a later plan or apply does. If it can't apply a rule cleanly, it shows the full drift instead, and anything it hides is still counted and labeled. It only masks what you name, so if the same resource drifted somewhere else you still see it and the check still fails. That's the one thing the refresh-only plus jq route can't do without a config change, and it's the part I've built.

The command itself is small.

 

A few specifics.

- It's strictly read-only. It forces refresh-only and rejects -destroy and -refresh=false (without a refresh it would report "no drift" regardless of the real state), and it can't apply or destroy under any arguments, which a plan-based check can't promise.
- Exit codes are 0 no drift, 1 error, 2 drift. The 2 lines up with what plan -detailed-exitcode already means. There's no "drift plus pending config" case to worry about, since refresh-only never looks at config changes, and if the refresh itself falls over that's just an error (1).
- In -json the only new thing is a drift_summary message with changed/deleted/total/ignored. resource_drift is the existing message, untouched.

terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode -json already handles detection and gives a clean exit code, so this isn't about finding drift. It's about being able to suppress expected drift per run, and having one read-only command to reach for instead of that flag combination.

On scope, in case it matters for the decision, this is a CLI-layer change with nothing touched in Terraform Core or the backends. I'll share the full diff when there's a PR.

On shape, the real alternative is hanging -ignore (and a drift-scoped exit code) off plan -refresh-only instead of a new command, and honestly I'd be fine with that. The catch is plan still can't promise read-only (it takes -out) and its flag list is already long. Changing what plan -detailed-exitcode returns is off the table, since it'd break everyone relying on today's 0/1/2.

I've got a working implementation with tests and I've run it against a real AWS provider, so I'm glad to share the branch. But per the contributing guide I wanted to talk about direction before dropping code. The real question is do you want a read-only drift command with a suppression flag at all, or would you rather the suppression be a flag on plan -refresh-only? Since -ignore is the whole reason for the command, I'd put it in v1, though I'm happy to stage its surface (resource-level first, attribute-level as a follow-up) if you'd prefer something smaller to start.

 References

- 28803 (closed, addressed by 30486): the drift-report noise problem; 30486 de-noised the plan view, -ignore is the per-run lever for a standalone check.
- 35226 (open): asks that plan exit 0 when everything matches, showing demand for drift-scoped exit semantics.

We rely on terraform validate as a quick check for reusable modules and their submodules before publishing them. Adding deprecated to an output now makes that check fail, even though the output is valid when the module is called by another module.

Could validate take an option that tells it we're checking a reusable module rather than a deployment root? We'd like to keep running validation directly against each module without removing deprecation declarations or building a wrapper just to make the check run.

This is related to hashicorp/terraform39207, which covers the same restriction during terraform test. This request is specifically about keeping the standalone terraform validate check available.

 Terraform version

 

No providers, credentials or cloud resources are needed for this example.

 Reproduction

main.tf:

 

Run from the module directory:

 

Validation exits with code 1:

 

Removing only the output's deprecated line makes validation pass. The input variable can remain deprecated. The hard failure here is the root-only restriction on the output, not an error caused by the deprecated input variable.

 Requested behavior

An explicit option such as terraform validate -reusable-module would let us say that this directory is intended to be called as a child module. The flag name is just a suggestion; a narrower option for the deprecated-output restriction would also help.

With that option, validate should accept deprecated outputs that are valid in a reusable module, retain any applicable deprecation warnings, and still fail on invalid syntax, bad references, type errors, invalid arguments and other genuine validation errors. The existing behavior should remain the default for normal root configurations, and this should not change plan or apply.

This isn't a request for a general "ignore errors" switch. We want the validation checks, without a failure that comes solely from treating a reusable module as a deployment root.

 Why this matters

The documentation describes validate as being "primarily useful for general verification of reusable modules": 

Validating examples is useful too, but it only checks modules that those examples actually reference. A separate check against each module directory is valuable, including for submodules that don't yet have an example. Writing wrappers also means supplying inputs and provider wiring just to run a static check.

I understand from hashicorp/terraform38309 that validate currently expects a complete root configuration, and that changing this may involve more than one output validation rule. That issue covers the similar problem with ephemeral outputs. An explicit reusable-module option would make the intended context clear without quietly changing how existing configurations are checked.
kept_issues.body:
We rely on `terraform validate` as a quick check for reusable modules and their submodules before publishing them. Adding `deprecated` to an output now makes that check fail, even though the output is valid when the module is called by another module.

Could `validate` take an option that tells it we're checking a reusable module rather than a deployment root? We'd like to keep running validation directly against each module without removing deprecation declarations or building a wrapper just to make the check run.

This is related to [hashicorp/terraform#39207](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/39207), which covers the same restriction during `terraform test`. This request is specifically about keeping the standalone `terraform validate` check available.

## Terraform version

```text
Terraform v1.16.2
on windows_amd64
```

No providers, credentials or cloud resources are needed for this example.

## Reproduction

`main.tf`:

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.15.0"
}

variable "name" {
  type       = string
  default    = "example"
  deprecated = "This input is kept for compatibility."
}

output "old_name" {
  value      = var.name
  deprecated = "This output is kept for compatibility."
}
```

Run from the module directory:

```powershell
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
```

Validation exits with code 1:

```text
Error: Root module output deprecated

  on main.tf line 13, in output "old_name":
  13:   deprecated = "This output is kept for compatibility."

Root module outputs cannot be deprecated, as there is no higher-level module to inform of the deprecation.
```

Removing only the output's `deprecated` line makes validation pass. The input variable can remain deprecated. The hard failure here is the root-only restriction on the output, not an error caused by the deprecated input variable.

## Requested behavior

An explicit option such as `terraform validate -reusable-module` would let us say that this directory is intended to be called as a child module. The flag name is just a suggestion; a narrower option for the deprecated-output restriction would also help.

With that option, `validate` should accept deprecated outputs that are valid in a reusable module, retain any applicable deprecation warnings, and still fail on invalid syntax, bad references, type errors, invalid arguments and other genuine validation errors. The existing behavior should remain the default for normal root configurations, and this should not change `plan` or `apply`.

This isn't a request for a general "ignore errors" switch. We want the validation checks, without a failure that comes solely from treating a reusable module as a deployment root.

## Why this matters

The documentation describes `validate` as being "primarily useful for general verification of reusable modules": https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/validate

Validating examples is useful too, but it only checks modules that those examples actually reference. A separate check against each module directory is valuable, including for submodules that don't yet have an example. Writing wrappers also means supplying inputs and provider wiring just to run a static check.

I understand from [hashicorp/terraform#38309](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/38309) that `validate` currently expects a complete root configuration, and that changing this may involve more than one output validation rule.  Use Cases

In large enterprise Terraform deployments (1,000 to 5,000+ resources, modules, and providers), executing terraform plan and terraform apply allocates significant heap memory during Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) walks in internal/dag/walk.go.

Profiling large graph walks (pprof & b.ReportAllocs()) reveals that graph execution creates ~18–20 heap object allocations per node every time Walker.Walk() runs. On a 2,500-node graph, a single walk allocates ~5.8 MB of RAM across 50,457 separate heap allocations.

Reducing these redundant memory allocations improves overall CLI throughput and decreases memory pressure on execution environments with memory constraints (such as CI/CD runners, Terraform Cloud / Enterprise worker agents, and local developer machines).

 Attempted Solutions

We profiled the Walker.Walk engine in internal/dag/walk.go across Linear, Diamond, and Grid graph topologies and identified 3 key sources of unnecessary allocations:

1. Map Re-allocation: w.vertexMap, w.diagsMap, w.upstreamFailed, and info.deps are initialized without capacity hints, causing Go to re-allocate internal hash tables as vertices are added.
2. Redundant Map Duplication: In Walk(), info.deps was stored as map[Vertex]chan struct{}. Because Go maps are invariant, passing info.deps to waitDeps(..., map[Vertex]<-chan struct{}) forced a manual map creation (make(map...)) and key-by-key copy loop for every node in g.edgesFrom.
3. Dummy Channel Allocations for Root Nodes: For nodes without dependencies (info.DepsCh == nil), walkVertex allocated a dummy channel (make(chan bool, 1)), wrote true to it, and closed it just to satisfy the select statement.

 Proposal

We propose 3 non-breaking internal optimizations in internal/dag/walk.go:

1. Pre-allocate map capacities using g.vertices.Len() hints for vertexMap, diagsMap, and upstreamFailed, and depsSet.Len() for info.deps.
2. Update walkerVertex.deps type to map[Vertex]<-chan struct{}. This enables implicit channel type-casting on map insertion and allows passing info.deps directly into go w.waitDeps(...) with zero map allocations and zero copy loops.
3. Directly evaluate root node dependencies: Replace dummy channel allocations with an if info.DepsCh != nil check in walkVertex.

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Linear Graph (1,000 nodes) | Time / Memory | 4.14 ms / 2.26 MB | 3.23 ms / 1.69 MB | ⚡ 22.0% faster / 25.4% less RAM |

| Diamond Graph (1,000 nodes) | Time / Memory | 6.60 ms / 2.70 MB | 4.14 ms / 2.00 MB | ⚡ 37.2% faster / 25.8% less RAM |
| Diamond Graph (1,000 nodes) | Allocs / op | 20,937 allocs | 17,345 allocs | ⚡ 17.1% fewer allocs |
| Grid Mesh (2,500 nodes) | Time / Memory | 11.64 ms / 5.83 MB | 8.92 ms / 4.72 MB | ⚡ 23.3% faster / 19.0% less RAM |
| Grid Mesh (2,500 nodes) | Allocs / op | 50,457 allocs | 43,332 allocs | ⚡ 14.1% fewer allocs |

Terraform Version

 

 Use Cases

We manage our MWAA environments with Terraform. We need to upgrade from Airflow 2.11.x to 3.x. Amazon MWAA now supports native in-place major-version upgrades (with an automatic metadata-DB snapshot and rollback), but the aws_mwaa_environment resource still forces a destroy/recreate when the major version changes. This means Terraform deletes the existing environment and its metadata database instead of performing the in-place upgrade the service now supports, which is unacceptable for production environments.

 Attempted Solutions

Upgrading to the latest hashicorp/aws provider does not help — the ForceNew-on-major-version logic is still present in the current provider code:

customdiff.ForceNewIf("airflow_version", func(...) bool {
 return oldVersion.Segments()[0] < newVersion.Segments()[0]
})

The only working path today is to upgrade out-of-band (console / aws mwaa update-environment), set lifecycle { ignore_changes = [airflow_version] }, and then reconcile Terraform state so it doesn't plan a replacement.

 Proposal

Update aws_mwaa_environment so a supported major-version upgrade is applied in-place via the UpdateEnvironment API rather than triggering ForceNew. The ForceNewIf guard was originally added to work around issue 21640, where the MWAA API rejected major upgrades. That limitation no longer applies now that MWAA supports in-place major-version upgrades, so the guard is outdated.
